label: Title
notes: Open by describing this chapter as the path-first reversal of Chapter 1. Previously the metric was the primitive data. In this lecture the admissible paths and their lengths become the objects that manufacture a distance, so the audience should listen for which distances are actually reachable by paths.

label: Chapter Question
notes: The chapter question is a two-way bridge. A length structure gives a distance by taking infima over path lengths, while any metric gives a curve length by partition sums. The lecture tracks when this round trip changes the geometry and when it returns the same intrinsic metric.

label: Length Structure Contract
notes: Use the contract language deliberately. A length structure is not just a curve with a number attached; it must behave well under restriction, concatenation, reparameterization, and local variation. These rules are what let path pieces assemble into a reliable metric.

label: Infimum Distance
notes: The infimum formula is where path geometry becomes distance. If two points can be joined by admissible curves, their distance is the cheapest length among those curves. If they cannot be joined, the induced distance is infinite, echoing the component picture from Chapter 1.

label: Diagnostic Examples
notes: Each diagnostic example should be read as a test of admissible routes. Manhattan travel changes balls into diamonds, obstacles force detours, circle geometry distinguishes chord from arc, and graph geometry makes edge routes rather than ambient straight lines decide distance.

label: Metric-Induced Curve Length
notes: Partition sums make curve length from a metric without coordinates. As the partition is refined, the polygonal approximation sees more of the curve's oscillation. The key point is that the supremum over all partitions is the definition, not just a numerical approximation.

label: Supremum Formula
notes: This formula slide is intentionally quiet. Name the partition, walk through consecutive samples, and then stress the supremum. The formula says that length is the largest total distance forced by every finite observation of the path in order.

label: Intrinsic Fixed Point
notes: Intrinsic metrics are fixed points of the metric-to-length-to-metric round trip. If arbitrarily fine paths recover exactly the original distance, then the metric already behaves as a path metric. If not, the induced intrinsic metric records extra route costs.

label: Dotted-Line Test
notes: The dotted-line test makes intrinsicness operational. We do not need a smooth path immediately; we can ask whether points can be connected by chains with very small jumps whose total length is close to the claimed distance. The notebook's dyadic chain keeps total length exact while max jump shrinks.

label: Midpoints
notes: A strict intrinsic space has exact midpoints, and repeated midpoint choices begin to look like a path. Completeness is what turns the dyadic limiting process into an actual curve, so midpoint constructions are also compactness and completeness tests in disguise.

label: Shortest Path vs Geodesic
notes: Separate shortest paths from geodesics carefully. A shortest path realizes the global distance. A geodesic may only minimize locally. The punctured-plane model has an infimum that is not attained, while the circle model shows a locally minimizing long arc that is not globally shortest.

label: Existence Roadmap
notes: The existence theorem should be taught as a mechanism. Compactness supplies convergent subsequences of almost-minimizing paths, lower semicontinuity prevents length from jumping down incorrectly, and completeness plus local compactness can produce compact closed balls where minimizers live.

label: Hausdorff Length
notes: For simple curves, length and one-dimensional Hausdorff measure agree because the image is traversed once. This is the bridge from the path language of Chapter 2 back to the scale-cover language introduced at the end of Chapter 1.

label: Multiplicity Warning
notes: The multiplicity warning prevents a common mistake. Hausdorff measure sees the image set, but length counts how the curve travels through that image. Traversing a segment forward and then backward doubles length while the image measure remains the same.

label: Lipschitz Speed
notes: Metric speed is the instantaneous version of path length. For Lipschitz curves the metric derivative exists almost everywhere, and integrating that speed recovers length. The speed graph turns the abstract derivative into a measurable rate.

label: Applied Diagnostic Lab
notes: The diagnostic lab is a practical checklist for unfamiliar spaces. If short chains fail, the space is not behaving intrinsically. If an infimum is never reached, compactness or completeness may be missing. If local minimizers stop being global, geodesic language must be used with care.

label: Summary
notes: Close with the round trip. Length structures produce distances, distances produce curve lengths, intrinsic metrics are fixed by this conversion, and shortest paths, Hausdorff length, and speed are three ways the path viewpoint becomes quantitative.
